method: A lockout policy lets an account accept a fixed number of failed attempts and then refuses authentication for a period. The model treats the attacker as persistent: while the account is open it submits failures at its attempt rate, so burning the threshold costs threshold / rate minutes, and then it waits out the lockout. One cycle therefore lasts threshold / rate + lockout minutes and yields exactly the threshold in guesses, so the sustained rate is threshold x 60 / cycle guesses per hour per account: five attempts, a fifteen minute lockout and 30 attempts a minute give a 15.167 minute cycle and 19.78 guesses an hour. The slowdown is the unthrottled rate divided by that throughput, which simplifies to 1 + lockout x rate / threshold, so once the wait dominates the threshold barely moves the result and a faster attacker buys almost nothing. Guesses per day multiply the hourly figure by 24, and the fleet figure multiplies by the number of targeted accounts, which is how a password spray spreads its budget across users. The counter reading follows the counting window: when the lockout is at least as long as the window every failure has aged out by unlock and the full allowance returns, so the cycle above is exact, while a shorter lockout can leave earlier failures inside the window at unlock, giving the attacker fewer than the threshold and making the reported throughput an upper bound, which the Counter at unlock row states. The model assumes one serial attacker per account, a threshold that counts consecutive failures, and no progressive delay, CAPTCHA, bot detection, IP-level limiting or identity-provider throttling; it says nothing about offline attacks, which are not rate limited at all. Inputs allow 1 to 1000 attempts, a lockout duration from 0.1 to 10080 minutes, a counting window from 1 to 10080 minutes, 0.01 to 100000 attempts a minute and 1 to 100000 accounts; blanks, non-numeric text, fractional counts and out-of-range values are refused with an actionable message. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4, Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management, Sec. 3.2.2 Rate Limiting (Throttling) — verifiers limit consecutive failed attempts on one account and may add a wait that grows toward the allowance
Microsoft Entra ID: Protect user accounts from attack with smart lockout — the lockout threshold and lockout duration are configured separately and enforced across data centers
